Parsimonious

par-suh-MOH-nee-uhs · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Parsimonious is unwilling to spend money or use resources, even when spending is clearly called for.

The city council's parsimonious budget left the public library open only two days a week, even though the town's finances were healthy.

Worked Example

The wealthy widow was so parsimonious that she still shopped exclusively at discount stores and clipped coupons for items she could easily afford without them.

Someone who can easily afford something but still refuses to spend on it, purely out of an unwillingness to part with money, is being parsimonious.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

stingy: Stingy is the everyday word for being unwilling to give or share — a stingy tipper, a stingy portion — and it points at meanness toward other people. Parsimonious is its formal cousin and goes further: a settled, grudging refusal to spend at all, even when spending is plainly needed.

tightfisted: Tightfisted pictures the habit vividly: a hand that will not open, a person reluctant to part with any money. Parsimonious carries an extra judgment — the refusal to spend is systematic and unreasonable, applied to budgets, councils, and households as readily as to loose change.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

generous: willing to give freely

extravagant: spending much more than necessary

Where it sits · how tight the grip on spending — frugal → parsimonious → miserly

frugal vs. parsimonious: Frugal is milder than parsimonious: a frugal shopper spends carefully and sensibly, while a parsimonious one is tighter still, refusing to part with money even when spending is needed.

miserly vs. parsimonious: Miserly is harsher than parsimonious: a parsimonious person is grudging about every expense, but a miserly one goes further, hoarding money with an almost obsessive grip.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — parsimoni- (parsimonia)

root — parsimoni- (parsimonia): thrift, frugality, from parcere, 'to spare' (Latin)

suffix — -ous

suffix — -ous: full of; possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Parsimonious comes from Latin parsimonia, 'thrift,' rooted in parcere, 'to spare.' Someone parsimonious is, quite literally, full of extreme sparing.

Use the root in a new word: parsimony

Use the root in a new word: parsimony: Even after winning the lottery, he lived with the same parsimony as before, refusing to move out of his one-room apartment.

Root Check

Word Choice

Parsimonious always carries a negative judgment -- it describes stinginess that has gone too far. Compare thrifty (later in this unit), which describes the same careful habits in a positive, admirable light, and a miser (also later), the kind of person who behaves parsimoniously.
